data.title: AI Takes On Cancer Detection From a Single Blood Draw (MEDS, ANT, GH, GRAL, NTRA, FRNM)
data.description:
Naples, Florida, November 20th, 2026, FinanceWire


Artificial intelligence is moving deeper into medicine, and cancer care is emerging as an important area of application. Machine learning models are being used to detect cancer earlier, help doctors select treatments, and monitor patients for signs of recurrence. Increasingly, these capabilities are being developed around a simple blood sample.

The companies building large AI models are pushing further into the field as well. Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) recently outlined how its Claude models are being incorporated into real-world drug development programs. In one example, six scientists at Generate Biomedicines used Claude Code to redesign a component of CAR T-cell therapy. The new design, about 70% shorter than the standard version, produced roughly 10 times as many receptors in lab tests and killed tumor cells more efficiently.

Meanwhile, blood-based cancer testing is moving beyond development and into commercialization. Tests are already available for colorectal cancer screening, multi-cancer early detection, and monitoring tumor DNA after a diagnosis. Newer approaches, including infrared spectroscopy, are also being developed to detect multiple cancer types from a single blood draw. Here are five stocks to take a closer look at.

DataMEDS AI, Inc. (NASDAQ:MEDS) is a healthcare technology company integrating pharmacy, laboratory, and telemedicine operations through its EinsteinRx AI platform. Its Helomics subsidiary operates a CLIA-certified precision oncology laboratory in Pittsburgh, built around the ChemoFx assay, which evaluates how a patient's live tumor cells respond to different chemotherapy agents. The company is now looking to expand its cancer diagnostics capabilities through blood-based testing and artificial intelligence.

DataMEDS has agreed to acquire certain assets from Todos Medical, including its Total Biochemical Infrared Analysis (TBIA) cancer testing platform and three tests: TM-B1 and TM-B2 for breast cancer, and TM-C1 for colorectal cancer. The acquisition introduces another approach to cancer detection that could complement Helomics' existing precision oncology capabilities.

TBIA uses Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy to analyze the biochemical characteristics of blood plasma and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. The platform digitizes the resulting data and applies machine learning to identify patterns that may distinguish healthy individuals from patients with cancer. Rather than relying exclusively on individual biomarkers detected through antibodies, the technology analyzes broader biochemical signatures. This approach could eventually support the detection of multiple cancer types and disease states using a single blood draw.

DataMEDS plans to install the spectroscopy platform at Helomics, where it can draw on the laboratory's existing infrastructure and oncologist network. The company intends to correlate TBIA results with biopsy and imaging data, conduct validation work, and pursue a commercial launch as a laboratory-developed test. It also sees potential for subsequent FDA submissions as the platform and its applications advance. The agreement additionally includes Todos Medical's license for the LymPro Alzheimer's diagnostic blood test.

Guardant Health, Inc. (NASDAQ:GH) is developing blood-based diagnostics across the cancer care continuum, including its Shield test for colorectal cancer screening. FDA-approved in 2024, Shield analyzes cell-free DNA for genetic and epigenetic changes associated with cancer. Guardant also offers precision oncology tests that help guide treatment decisions in patients with advanced cancer. Its third-quarter 2026 Shield volume reached approximately 83,000 tests, up 246% year over year, highlighting the growing adoption of blood-based screening.

GRAIL, Inc. (NASDAQ:GRAL) is focused on multi-cancer early detection through its Galleri test, which analyzes cell-free DNA from a single blood sample for cancer-associated methylation patterns. Machine learning helps identify potential cancer signals and predict their likely tissue of origin, guiding follow-up testing. Galleri is designed to detect signals associated with more than 50 cancer types, including cancers without widely recommended routine screening programs. GRAIL reported more than 56,000 tests in the third quarter of 2026, approximately 24% above the prior-year period, while an FDA advisory committee recently voted in favor of the test's safety, effectiveness, and overall benefit-risk profile.

Natera, Inc. (NASDAQ:NTRA) approaches cancer diagnostics through molecular residual disease testing. Its Signatera platform uses tumor-specific genetic information to track circulating tumor DNA in a patient's blood following a cancer diagnosis. This allows physicians to monitor for molecular signs of residual disease or recurrence that may not yet be visible through conventional imaging. Natera is also developing AI models that combine genomic sequencing, digital pathology, and longitudinal patient data to improve recurrence prediction. Oncology testing volume increased 60.9% year over year in the third quarter of 2026.

Freenome, Inc. (NASDAQ:FRNM) is developing blood-based cancer screening through a platform that combines artificial intelligence, machine learning, and multiomics. Its SimpleScreen CRC test received FDA approval in July 2026 for colorectal cancer screening in average-risk adults aged 45 and older, with Abbott holding exclusive U.S. commercialization rights. Abbott launched the test commercially in September, and Freenome launched SimpleScreen Lung in October. The company is also developing a broader multi-cancer detection approach, with an initial readout expected in mid-2027.

As AI becomes more integrated into pharmaceutical research and cancer diagnostics, these companies illustrate how the technology is being applied across different stages of medicine, from developing new treatments to detecting cancer, guiding therapy, and monitoring patients after treatment.

data.title: The AI Bubble Is Draining Market Liquidity, But Gold’s Fundamentals Remain Robust
data.description:
In my October 30 article, titled “The AI bubble is draining capital from other markets, including gold”, I explained how the artificial intelligence industry had become an enormous magnet for capital. Hundreds of billions of dollars were being mobilized to finance infrastructure whose future profitability remained largely unproven, while small-cap companies, industrial businesses and mining stocks were struggling to attract investors.

I focused on an especially dangerous mechanism: the market valuations of AI-related companies no longer simply reflected their growth prospects; they were gradually becoming an essential condition for financing that growth. The higher share prices climbed, the more capital these companies could raise to fund new data centers, thereby sustaining stock-market euphoria.

But this mechanism also works in reverse.

When valuations begin to fall, financing capacity deteriorates, lenders reassess the collateral available to them, and companies that depend most heavily on capital markets are forced to rethink their ambitions. This is precisely the risk we had identified.

The governance crisis currently engulfing Nvidia adds a new dimension to this vulnerability. Jensen Huang’s resignation, followed by statements hinting at a possible return, prompted an unusual show of activity in Silicon Valley. However, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly argued in favor of appointing a successor from outside the company, amid questions about technological ties with China.

Beyond the circumstances of this departure, which still require clarification, the situation highlights just how strategically important Nvidia has become to the United States. Jensen Huang was not simply running a semiconductor manufacturer: he embodied an ecosystem in which suppliers, customers and investors have increasingly close financial ties.

The market correction now gives us a sense of the risks involved. Since its October 6 peak, Nvidia has lost around $2 trillion in market capitalization, with its valuation falling from approximately $5.8 trillion to $3.8 trillion.

Of course, this does not mean that $2 trillion in cash has actually left the markets. But this destruction of financial wealth can reduce the value of assets used as collateral, limit investors’ borrowing capacity and trigger forced selling across other asset classes.

This is how a stock-market correction concentrated in a handful of major technology companies can gradually turn into a broad-based contraction in liquidity.

The Fed cannot offset the destruction of financial wealth

Some investors are now counting on the Federal Reserve to stabilize the markets. Yet the amounts involved illustrate the limits of monetary intervention.

The Fed plans to reinvest around $14 billion in Treasury securities between November 16 and December 11, a negligible amount compared with the $2 trillion wiped off Nvidia’s market capitalization. These figures are not directly comparable, of course, since the Fed’s reinvestments are not intended to offset stock-market losses. However, they give an idea of the gap between the monetary operations currently planned and the scale of the ongoing repricing of financial assets.

More importantly, providing reserves to banks does not necessarily restore their appetite for risk. A bank may have ample liquidity and still refuse to finance a data-center operator whose collateral is losing value.

The problem is particularly concerning for neocloud providers, whose business models depend on continuously securing new financing. CoreWeave bonds are reportedly now yielding close to 15%, while certain Nebius convertible bonds are trading at around 70% of their face value.

With borrowing costs rising so sharply, profitability prospects could deteriorate quickly. The major hyperscalers still have balance sheets strong enough to absorb some of this pressure, but the most heavily indebted operators could find themselves in a much more difficult position.

Here we see the same mechanisms that emerged during the telecom bubble: a genuine technological revolution, but infrastructure financed on the basis of growth and profitability assumptions that the markets eventually begin to question.

The question is no longer simply how many GPUs Nvidia will be able to sell, but who will still be able to borrow the money to buy them, and at what cost.

Gold is correcting under liquidity pressure, but demand remains resilient

The recent correction in precious metals needs to be understood in this context.

In October, gold fell 6.8%, ending the month at around $3,875 an ounce, while silver lost 18.7% and the leading gold-mining stocks declined by nearly 12%.

At first glance, this may seem paradoxical. Concerns about financing the AI industry, deteriorating credit conditions and mounting sovereign-debt tensions should, in theory, make gold more attractive.

But when a stock-market correction triggers deleveraging, investors do not sell only the losing positions. They also dump their most liquid assets to rebuild cash reserves and meet margin calls.

Gold then becomes a source of liquidity to cover losses incurred elsewhere.

We saw this phenomenon in 2008 and again in March 2020. In both cases, gold initially corrected during the broad liquidation phase before regaining its role as a safe haven when central banks were forced to intervene.

But one feature sets the current correction apart: falling prices have not been accompanied by a collapse in investment demand.

At the end of October, gold-backed ETF holdings stood at around 100.97 million ounces, even surpassing their February levels. Silver-backed ETFs also recorded an increase in their physical holdings, adding nearly 4.9 million ounces over the month.

In other words, prices fell sharply while the quantities of metal held by these investment vehicles remained resilient.

This divergence suggests that the correction has been driven more by position adjustments in derivatives markets, systematic strategies and short-term liquidity needs than by a broad withdrawal of long-term investors.

Quantitative funds and trend-following strategies, in particular, reduced their exposure to gold as certain technical thresholds were breached. According to some estimates, these market participants’ short positions were already approaching their usual limits by mid-October.

This development matters. Once excessive speculative positioning has been largely unwound, the market may become more sensitive to an improvement in financial conditions, although this does not necessarily mean that a bottom has already been reached.

China is absorbing some of the selling from Western markets

Another revealing factor is the behavior of Chinese buyers.

While Western investors were reducing their exposure to gold, premiums in Shanghai remained high, pointing to physical demand capable of absorbing some of the metal being sold internationally.

The divergence between the two markets has become striking. Over a rolling ten-week period, the correlation between an indicator combining Western gold positioning and Shanghai premiums is said to have fallen to around −0.97.

This figure does not mean that China mechanically absorbs every ounce sold in the West. Nevertheless, it shows that the two indicators have recently moved in almost opposite directions: while Western financial investors were reducing their positions, premiums in the Chinese market pointed to sustained physical demand.

This distinction between the financial market and the physical market is becoming essential.

On Western markets, prices are heavily influenced in the short term by futures contracts, options, quantitative strategies and portfolio arbitrage. In China, physical demand is driven more by concerns relating to wealth preservation, monetary considerations and savings diversification.

The persistent weakness of China’s property market, difficulties in domestic credit markets and uncertainty surrounding economic growth are prompting some savers to seek assets whose value does not depend directly on the solvency of a financial intermediary.

Gold also benefits from central banks’ desire to diversify their reserves in an increasingly fragmented geopolitical environment.

We are therefore seeing a revealing trend: Western investors might sell gold to obtain dollars, but other market participants buy gold precisely to reduce their dependence on those same dollars.

This divergence could become one of the market’s main sources of support once liquidation pressures begin to ease.

Sovereign debt is gradually reinforcing gold’s monetary role

The recent correction should not obscure the broader transformation in the macroeconomic environment.

In October, gold faced a particularly unfavorable combination of factors: rising US real interest rates, a stronger dollar, energy-related inflationary pressures and a tightening of global financial conditions.

The US 10-year real yield briefly approached 3%, while the nominal yield exceeded 5.3%. In such an environment, the higher opportunity cost of holding an asset that generates no income makes gold less attractive to some investors.

But this rise in interest rates also reveals a much deeper vulnerability.

Developed countries must finance substantial structural deficits even as the cost of their debt rises. France is a particularly worrying example: its 10-year sovereign yield exceeded 5%, while the yield spread over German bonds reached around 174 basis points at the end of October.

The problem extends well beyond France. The United States, the United Kingdom and Japan are facing, to varying degrees, higher financing needs and increased sensitivity of their public finances to interest rates.

For investors, this raises a fundamental question: can sovereign bonds continue to serve simultaneously as reserve assets, financial collateral and protection against crises?

When the sustainability of public debt itself becomes a source of concern, physical gold once again demonstrates the full relevance of one of its fundamental characteristics: it is not the liability of any government and does not depend on any issuer’s ability to repay its debt.

Silver and mining stocks: an even sharper correction

Silver suffered a much steeper correction than gold in October, falling by nearly 19%. This underperformance can be explained by a combination of contracting liquidity, the metal’s inherently higher volatility and its sensitivity to the outlook for industrial activity.

As a result, the gold-to-silver ratio has risen to around 79, well above its long-term historical average, generally estimated at 60:

This level is not in itself a buy signal, but it highlights the extent of silver’s relative underperformance.

The situation is all the more interesting because silver-backed ETF holdings increased during the correction. From their July lows, these investment vehicles are said to have accumulated nearly 19.5 million additional ounces by the end of October.

Some investors appear to be taking advantage of lower prices to increase their exposure to the metal, while derivatives markets continue to exert downward pressure on prices.

Mining stocks, for their part, remain particularly vulnerable during episodes of deleveraging. They combine exposure to metal prices with sensitivity to equity markets and, in the case of small-cap companies, often limited liquidity.

But this correction is also widening valuation gaps between companies with tangible assets, identified reserves and sometimes substantial cash flows, and technology companies whose valuations are still largely based on expectations of future revenue.

This divergence is likely to persist as long as investors continue to reduce their overall exposure to risk.

Nevertheless, it could pave the way for a much more favorable phase of capital reallocation toward real assets once financing pressures begin to ease.

The immediate risk for gold remains another wave of forced liquidations. But its main source of support over the medium term could lie precisely in the financial consequences of the AI bubble bursting.

The real question, then, is not simply how far technology stocks may fall, but when the contraction in liquidity will stop weighing on the gold price and begin to strengthen its role as a benchmark monetary asset.

data.title: Australia Employment Declines Below Consensus
data.description:
-43.5K vs. +25.5K in October, m/m; unemployment rate rises +0.2 ppts, against no change consensus. Talk of recession ensues.

Figure 1: Australian employment 15+ (blue, left log scale), unemployment rate, % (red, right scale), both s.a. Source: ABS.

While the labor market deteriorated (surprisingly) in October, GDP data only extends to Q2 (next release December 2). The October nowcast from the Melbourne Institute indicates +0.4% q/q growth for Q3; the next nowcast is set for a week from now.

Figure 2: Australian GDP (bold black), Melbourne Institute October nowcast (red +), RBA November Statement of Monetary Policy forecast (light blue square), all in mn.Ch.2024$, on log scale. Source: ABS, Melbourne Institute, RBA. 

Hard to see a recession starting if the nowcast proves accurate — although the October nowcast was based on earlier data, and even when reported, GDP will be revised repeatedly.

Value added in industrial output (sum of mining, utilities and manufacturing) and disposable income are available at quarterly frequency. Disposable income is leveling off, while industrial output is flat after a brief recovery.

Figure 3: Australian real industrial output (blue, left log scale), real disposable income (red, right log scale), both mn.Ch.2024$. Source: ABS.

Finally, conditions and sentiment indicators that might predict a recession (neither of these span the 1990 recession) are trending downward.

Figure 4: Australia NAB Business Conditions indicators (blue, left scale), and Wespac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment (red, right scale). Source: RBA.

The Guardian characterized the outlook:

Australia may already have “one foot in recession” after unemployment surged to 4.9% in October, from 4.7%, in a shock increase that will add to rising worries that this year’s five interest rate hikes have pushed the economy past a tipping point.

Since the rate hikes were set to contain inflationary pressures due to elevated oil prices, it makes me wonder: how many countries will be tipped into recession by Mr. Trump’s war.

data.title: Gold Faces Heavy Selling Pressure As Key Support Fails
data.description:
Source: DepositPhotos

Gold has experienced serious capitulation over the last few days, with prices breaking below 3,700, an area we had been tracking as potential support. However, this level has so far failed to produce any meaningful rebound, keeping the short-term outlook bearish.

XAUUSD(gold) 4H Chart

We could still see some stabilization, especially if the current fifth wave is extending and approaching its final stages. However, the trend remains bearish until proven otherwise. Ideally, we would need to see a clear bullish reversal, supported by an impulsive five-wave rally back above 3,868, the previous swing low, to gain confidence that an important bottom is forming.

Such a recovery would also invalidate the alternate bearish wave count, which suggests that the current decline could still be unfolding in wave three rather than wave five.

Therefore, it is still too early to call a bottom. If selling pressure continues, the bigger picture on the weekly chart highlights another very important support area around 3,500, which could become the next potential downside target.

Big Picture

On a higher-degree time frame, gold still appears to be trading within a broader impulsive bullish structure, but it is currently undergoing a wave four correction that could gradually approach completion later this year. The ideal strong support zone is between 3,900 and 3,200, where we will be watching for potential signs of stabilization and the next bullish reversal opportunity.

data.title: Indian Rupee Hits Fresh Seven-Month Low On Strong FIIs Buying Momentum
data.description:
• The Indian Rupee posts a fresh seven-month high against the US Dollar, with the USD/INR pair sliding to near 92.70.

  • Indian stock market continues to attract foreign money on the back of lower oil prices and global AI unwinding.

  • The US Dollar Index extends its rally amid a hawkish Fed narrative.

The Indian Rupee (INR) extends its upside run against the US Dollar (USD) on Friday, strengthened by the continuous inflow of foreign funds amid global Artificial Intelligence (AI) unwinding and lower oil prices.

During the day, the USD/INR pair posts a fresh seven-month low near 92.70.

On Thursday, Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) remain net buyers in the Indian stock market again and raised their stake in equities worth Rs. 7,411.41 crore. So far in November, FIIs has made investments worth Rs. 1,01,640.97 crore.

What has improved India’s appeal in recent weeks?

According to The Economic Times (ET), India has been described as an “anti-AI” trade because it was left out of much of the global AI rally and has limited direct exposure to the AI supply chain. Any unwinding of crowded AI-linked positions could therefore encourage investors to rotate into other emerging markets, including India and Brazil.

Analysts at DBS said in a note that “regional equity plays that have been relatively less exposed to the AI-play this year appear to be benefiting in the initial phase of re-allocation”.

Meanwhile, lower oil prices due to rising supply of energy products from the Middle East have also increased the appeal of India.

In the opening trade, the MCX Crude Oil contract expiring on December 18 is close to its over 11-week low of Rs. 7,619 posted on Wednesday.

Strategists at Danske Bank highlight that the recent sell-off in crude has been substantial, with “oil prices… down around 20% this month,” as the market responds to “recovering supply from the Middle East” and growing “expectations that US President Donald Trump will avoid renewed full-scale hostilities with Iran.”

Investors shrug off rally in US Dollar

The continuous rally in the Indian Rupee against the US Dollar despite the US Dollar Index (DXY) hitting fresh highs every trading day in over a week reflects sheer strength in the Indian currency.

As of writing, the USD Index is marginally lower to near 103.78 from its fresh 19-month high of around 104.00 posted the previous day.

Analysts at MUFG/BTMU note that “almost all Fed officials have judged that additional rate hikes would likely be appropriate in the months ahead to bring inflation back to the 2% target.” They add that “markets continue to fully price in a 25bps hike in December, three 25bps hikes by June next year, leaving elevated US rates and a resilient Dollar.

Technical Analysis: USD/INR sees more downside towards 92.50

In the daily chart, USD/INR trades at 92.71, maintaining a bearish near-term tone as it holds beneath the nine-period exponential moving average (EMA) at 93.57. The pair continues to slide away from this dynamic resistance, while the Relative Strength Index (RSI) at 22.6 sits in oversold territory, hinting that downside momentum is stretched but not yet reversed.

On the topside, the 9-period EMA at 93.57 is the first resistance to clear for any recovery attempt, and a sustained move above this level would ease immediate bearish pressure. On the downside, the pair could extend its decline towards 92.20.

data.title: Silver Price Forecast: Failed Recovery Leaves Market Vulnerable
data.description:
The silver market continues to see a lot of noisy trading, particularly to the downside, as there are major headwinds out there to keep the silver market down. The most obvious reason is real rates.

Silver

The silver market initially tried to rally during Thursday’s trading session but then gave back gains again as we tried to cross above the $45 level. The $48 level after that has a certain amount of resistance built into it as well, followed by the 50-day EMA. This is a market that really has no signs of strength, and there are various areas above that could cause massive issues.

Ultimately, this is a market that I think continues to see a lot of pressure, not only from possibly forced liquidations, but also because real rates in America continue to pay you quite well. If that is going to be the case, it is very likely that traders will be watching any rally as an opportunity to start shorting silver again.

The psychology of $50

The $50 level being broken through over the last couple of days is a big deal. That was a major ceiling for decades, which was just recently broken, and we are already below it again. I think silver has further to go to the downside. Clearly, there are no signs of real strength.

Longer term, I love silver. I think it will be a great investment. But right now, in this environment, until those real rates come down, it is going to be very difficult for silver to pick up strength. It is so sensitive to rates, even more so than gold. Of course, the strong U.S. dollar is doing it no favors as well, which is all intertwined. At this point, this is a market that remains fragile at best, horrible at worst.

data.title: Anthropic’s Debut Failed To Reverse Investor Skepticism Toward AI Sector Profitability
data.description:
The US equity markets closed sharply lower on Thursday as the record-breaking market debut of Anthropic failed to alleviate investor concerns regarding profitability and elevated debt levels across the artificial intelligence sector. By the end of the session, the Dow Jones (US30) had fallen by 2.19%, the S&P 500 (US500) declined by 2.02%, and the Nasdaq (US100) dropped by 2.21%.

Shares of Anthropic (ticker: ANT), which raised a record $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history at $83 per share, opened at $111.50 (+34%) but surrendered a significant portion of those gains during the session, closing at $97.17 (+17.1%). The sell-off spread across both semiconductor manufacturers and cloud hyperscalers as investors questioned whether massive AI infrastructure investments would generate sufficient returns. Nvidia shares declined a further 3.3% amid management turmoil following the resignation of Jensen Huang, while AMD plunged 7.7% after Hunterbrook Capital issued a sell recommendation citing risks related to China exposure and customer financing. Among technology megacaps, Amazon fell by 3.9%, and Meta lost 3.3%.

In November, the Mexican peso (MXN) weakened to around 19 per US dollar, its lowest level since June 2025, following the release of minutes from Banco de México’s latest policy meeting, which left the door open for further monetary easing. Additional pressure on the currency stems from diverging interest-rate trajectories. With the Federal Reserve expected to raise rates in December, the yield differential between Mexico and the United States continues to narrow, reducing the attractiveness of peso-denominated carry-trade positions.

European equity indices erased their early gains and closed lower for a fifth consecutive trading session as investors continued to reduce risk exposure. Germany’s DAX (DE40) fell by 1.06%, France’s CAC 40 (FR40) declined by 0.81%, Spain’s IBEX 35 (ES35) lost 0.97%, and the UK’s FTSE 100 (UK100) ended the day down 0.93%. Sector-wise, pharmaceutical companies experienced some of the heaviest pressure, with shares of Sanofi and Bayer falling nearly 3%, while technology services stocks also remained under significant pressure.

The US natural gas prices (XNG) corrected lower to $3.33 per MMBtu from the 11-month high of $3.372 reached on November 18 as market participants reassessed supply and inventory conditions. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), commercial gas inventories increased by 20 billion cubic feet to 3.882 trillion cubic feet during the week ended November 13, below consensus expectations for an increase of 25-27 billion cubic feet. Despite the smaller-than-expected inventory build, storage levels remain comfortable and stand 2.1% above the five-year seasonal average, compared with a 2.0% surplus a week earlier, limiting further upside in prices.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 (JP225) advanced 0.71%, China’s FTSE China 50 gained 0.31%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng (HK50) fell 1.95%, while Australia’s ASX 200 (AU200) closed Thursday’s session down 1.04%.

The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) left its benchmark Loan Prime Rates (LPRs) unchanged at record lows for an eighteenth consecutive month since May 2025, fully in line with market expectations. The one-year LPR, the reference rate for most corporate and household loans, remained at 3.0%, while the five-year LPR, the benchmark for mortgage lending, stayed at 3.5%. The decision to pause rate cuts came despite signs of weakening economic momentum in October, when both industrial production and retail sales growth slowed while residential property prices continued to decline.

data.title: Cheaper Gasoline Is Coming
data.description:
James Thorne of Wellington Altus tweeted an important graph and commentary worth reviewing. The US 3-2-1 crack spread, which approximates what a refiner earns by turning three barrels of crude into two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of distillates, has fallen 36% in six weeks, from $65.56 on October 9 to $41.90 on November 17. As he puts it, “the glut has moved downstream.”

The evidence supports his view. Fat profit margins enticed refiners to run at maximum capacity and boost their profits as much as possible. As one would think, with falling crack spreads, gasoline and diesel prices are falling faster than crude as supply rises rapidly. AAA shows the national gasoline price average near $3.75, down roughly 13% in a month, and the gasoline ETF UGA has dropped about 21% month to date. Gasoline futures have fallen about 45% over the last two months from $3.63 on September 24 to its current level of $2.50. Because retail pump prices lag wholesale/futures by weeks, the AAA pump price should fall further.

Over the last four decades, the 3-2-1 spread averages roughly $12 a barrel with a median near $8. On an EIA spot basis, it averaged $68 in September, the richest month since 2006, and even after the sharp drop to the low $40s, it remains well above average. In other words, spreads have plenty of room to decline as refiners still have the financial incentive to produce as much gasoline and diesel as possible.

Gasoline remains more than a dollar above year-ago levels, so annual price comparisons will likely remain inflationary until spring. However, the Fed Funds futures markets are pricing roughly 75 basis points of further tightening. Hiking into falling energy prices looks to us like the Fed is fighting yesterday’s war.

Market Trading Update

Yesterday, we compared Nvidia’s earnings risk to the “safety” premium investors pay for Walmart. Today, I want to return to the Santa Claus rally we discussed in Tuesday’s commentary, but from a different angle. The question isn’t whether it shows up. It’s WHEN.

Goldman’s flow desk made a sharp point this week. Two-month seasonal averages are too blunt for this tape. Their S&P 500 path, going back to 1928, shows a Thanksgiving ramp, a stall in early December, and a second-leg higher. Read off their chart, roughly 80% of the average gain arrives after December 14. We ran the same test on S&P 500 total returns since 2003, and the shape holds.

The sequence makes sense once you look at who is trading. Retail buying and corporate buybacks typically carry stocks into early December. Then the plumbing gets in the way. Many mutual funds set capital gains distribution record dates around the second week of December, and some taxable investors sell ahead of them to dodge the bill. Tax-loss selling peaks. Goldman expects the buyback window to close around December 13, the Fed meets December 8 and 9, and December 18 brings quarterly options expiration. Once that pile-up clears, managers dress up their books for year-end reporting, and the Santa Claus rally gets its second wind.

Here’s where it gets interesting. Since 2010, the December 5 to 14 window has lost 0.27% on average and finished higher in only 7 of 16 years. In most years, it’s a pause. In 2011, 2014, 2015, and 2018, it was a 3%-3.6% hit.

Goldman’s base rates for years like this one, when the VIX starts mid-November at 18 or higher, deserve respect. The median drawdown inside the window was 3%, and the year-end gain averaged just 1.34%. With the S&P 500 closing Wednesday near 7,318, about 6% below its October 6 record, we’re already living part of that script.

We should not dismiss that hedge funds and CTAs are very underweight technology stocks, which does provide a potential tailwind. However, there is always the risk that they choose to remain sidelined through year-end.

Here is how to play the next few weeks.

  • First, don’t chase the Thanksgiving pop. If the ramp shows up, use strength into early December to trim winners back to target weight and rebuild cash.

  • Secondly, put that cash to work into mid-December weakness, ahead of the stretch that historically does the heavy lifting.

That’s the playbook in our Equity Conservative Growth and Equity Aggressive Growth models. The calendar rewards patience, not urgency. Such is the nature of seasonal trading.

Santa usually shows up, but if you lose too much before then, the gift of Christmas doesn’t really matter.

Fed Worries About AI Financing Web

The October FOMC minutes, released yesterday, contain a passage worth focusing on. Per the minutes, most participants “observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly,” and much of that growth “had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures.”

A few participants noted that AI exposures were “becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms.” They also flagged off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing among AI firms as potential loss amplifiers.

We wrote about this last week in Nvidia Circular Financing: Who Is At Risk?, where we traced the guarantees, residual value support, and off-balance-sheet lease backstops that Nvidia was providing to support the AI buildout and, in turn, chip purchases. Our conclusion was that the companies most at risk were those like CoreWeave, with high interest rates and seemingly losing access to the capital markets. The Fed agrees.

Here is why this mention in the minutes is important. The Fed does not casually put a sector’s financing structure into its minutes. Describing AI debt as opaque and concentrated moves it from market chatter to a documented financial stability concern, and that may be the first step toward supervisory attention.

The tension between Fed policy and the AI debt is worth appreciating. In the minutes, almost all participants judged that “further action to raise the target range” would “likely be appropriate,” and two members suggested, “an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting.” The Fed is now identifying a leveraged, opaque, and concentrated credit structure while preparing to raise its cost of funding. We will watch credit spreads, not equity prices, for any potential fallout. The graphic below is courtesy of The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: Ripple Hangovers Are The Worst
data.description:
THE RIPPLE EFFECT

Long before the advent of cryptocurrencies, the term ripple (noun) meant "a small wave or slight movement on a surface, especially water; or a light, spreading sound, emotion, or effect". (Google AI Overview)

Example: Dropping a pebble into a pond of still water creates ripples which flow gently across the pond.

In the 1960s, Ripple was a carbonated, sweet wine produced by E. & J. Gallo Winery. Light carbonation and a variety of fruit flavors spurred its initial acceptance; however, one additional factor greatly added to its popularity. Ripple was very inexpensive. Originally costing $ 1 per bottle, it was often the drink of choice during the "pop wine" era of the 1970s.

Intended as a cheap table wine, its frequent misuse by those who were inclined to overindulge led to serious consequences. Those consequences were similar to those experienced by others who drank too much and are commonly referred to as a hangover.

For those who preferred the popular, cheap drink of choice, the term "hangover" was exchanged for the more descriptive "ripple effect". The movements, however, were not slight and the undulations were anything but gentle. 

RIPPLE

At one time, Ripple (XRP-X)appeared to be a darling child of the cryptocurrency progeny. Deliberate and conscious attention by various personalities and investors, as well as favorable publicity, popularized the lesser-known Ripple, one of Bitcoin's younger brethren.

The benefits translated to outsized price performance.

Between the end of October 2024 and mid-July 2025, the price of Ripple soared from $.50 to a high of $3.65. The more than seven-fold increase in less than nine months amounted to 630%.  The future looked bright, and Ripple was expected to continue outperforming other cryptocurrencies. 

Unfortunately, the $3.65 price is still the high, and price action since then has been steeply downhill. After breaking the $1 mark briefly, then rallying almost 50%, Ripple recently traded at $.89, down more than 75% from its all-time high set sixteen months ago. 

The hangover must be quite awful for Ripple investors and enthusiasts, and the possibilities for dealing with it are harsh. 

Short-term: 1) Stop consuming (buying) large quantities of cheap wine (Ripple). 2) Don't expect a rapid recovery. 3) Expect the hangover symptoms to worsen. 

Long-term: 1) See number 1 above. 2) Expect a long and winding road, and lower prices before price stabilization occurs. 3) Get lots of rest. You are going to need it. 

Other cryptocurrencies are exhibiting weakness and vulnerability, much as they have since summer 2025. Bitcoin (BTC.X) is the lead dog in the crypto markets, but Ripple is leading the way down in price.

data.title: Heavy Selling Is Clustering - What To Expect Next
data.description:
Market Breadth Watch: Heavy Selling Is Clustering: What To Expect Next

Two volume readings flashed the same message this week.

Two different volume readings flashed the same message this week: the selling is coming in clusters, not single days. One measures the whole NYSE, the other SPY’s own trading. Below is what each one shows and what SPY did after similar stretches before.

1. NYSE down volume: four heavy days in six sessions

On Thursday (Nov 19), 86% of NYSE volume went into falling stocks and 82% of issues declined. On its own that is a heavy day, not a rare one. What stands out is the clustering: it was the fourth day of 78% or more NYSE down volume in the last six sessions (Nov 12: 80%, Nov 16: 78%, Nov 17: 79%, Nov 19: 86%).

What SPY did after heavy NYSE selling, 1998 to 2026

2. SPY’s own volume: three heavy down days in four sessions

SPY fell 2.0% on Thursday to $715.87 on 76 million shares, 1.65 times its 50-day average. It was the third down day in four sessions with volume at 1.5 times the average or more (Nov 16: 1.54x, Nov 17: 1.57x, Nov 19: 1.65x).

SPY’s volume shows three such clusters since June. In June, SPY made its low (about 725) inside the cluster and rallied to 778 by early August. The Oct 30 to Nov 5 cluster included the biggest volume day of the period (126 million shares, 3 times the average) and was followed by a bounce to 760. This one is different: all three heavy days are down days, and SPY is at a new low for the period with no bounce yet.

What SPY did after its own heavy-volume selling, 1993 to 2026

What stands out

Both say the same thing

Whether you count heavy selling across the NYSE or in SPY itself, a cluster of heavy days was followed by better-than-normal returns: about twice the normal 20-day gain and better odds. Repeated selling tends to use up the sellers.

More selling usually comes first

After an 85%+ NYSE down-volume day, another one followed within 10 sessions more than half the time (106 of 189), and the median low over the next 20 days was 1.9% below that day’s close. In SPY’s own clusters the median case also saw a close 2.4% lower within 20 days. Feb 25, 2020 was one of those cases, and it came before the worst of that crash.

Not a guaranteed low

The edge shows up over one to three months, not in a straight line. The fall of 2023 had a similar stretch: after the third heavy NYSE day (Oct 3), more heavy days followed and SPY fell another 2.6% over three weeks before the low on Oct 27.

What to watch

An up day on heavy volume

In SPY, a heavy-volume up day would be the first sign the selling is being absorbed, as on Jun 11 and Nov 4. More heavy down days at lower closes would mean the cluster is still building.

The oversold gauge turning up inside the cluster

The oversold gauge I track is deep in its low zone, in the lowest 1.3% of all readings since 2004. Its strongest buy signal in back-tests is the day its slower reading turns back up from oversold, and that has not happened yet.

When the turn came during an NYSE selling cluster (three or more days of 78%+ NYSE down volume within six sessions), SPY was higher 20 days later in 22 of 25 cases since 2007, by about 5% on average (3.7% without the 2009 and 2020 rebounds), against about 3% for the turn on its own. The misses were Oct 2008 (-8.6%), Jun 2010 (-2.0%) and Oct 2023 (-0.5%). 25 cases is a small sample, so I treat it as a confirmation, not a system.

Timing matters

The six-session window moves forward each day and older heavy days drop out of it. With Nov 16, 17, and 19 in the window, a turn on Friday (Nov 20) or Monday (Nov 23) would still count. From Tuesday on it needs fresh 78%+ days to keep the cluster alive.

data.description:
GBP/USD fell to 1.3085 on Friday, remaining at its lowest level in almost a year. The main pressure on the pound comes from sharply rising expectations of further Fed tightening, which is supporting the US dollar.

Minutes from the October Fed meeting showed that the Fed is increasingly concerned about persistent inflation and acknowledges the need for additional rate hikes. Policymaker Christopher Waller called for more decisive action if price pressures continue to rise. Markets now estimate the probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December at 97.3%, with the chance of a 50-basis-point move at 2.7%.

In the UK, the situation is less straightforward. The Bank of England expects inflation to accelerate further by mid-2027 due to cumulative cost pressures, but some components of the October CPI proved fairly stable. Against this backdrop, markets have scaled back expectations of a BoE rate hike in December, further limiting support for the pound.

Yields on UK government bonds also fell following the inflation report, with the yield on 10-year gilts dropping to 5.29%. Although headline CPI reached 3.6% year-on-year, markets have become more cautious about further Bank of England tightening, adding to pressure on GBP/USD.

October UK retail sales will be the next key release, with zero month-on-month growth and 1.7% year-on-year growth expected. Stronger-than-expected data could temporarily support the pound, but the fundamental balance remains in the dollar’s favour due to much stronger expectations of Fed tightening.

Technical Analysis

The H4 GBP/USD chart remains in a downtrend. After a reversal in early November, the pair has formed a succession of lower highs and lows while remaining within the descending channel. The MACD signal line is below zero and pointing downwards, indicating continued downward momentum. The nearest target on H4 is 1.3024.

On the H1 GBP/USD chart, the pair rebounded from 1.3078 to approach 1.3125, where it had previously consolidated. For Friday, 20 November 2026, the baseline scenario assumes a test of 1.3125 from below. If resistance holds, a return to 1.3078 is likely. A break below this low would open the way towards 1.3024. Both Stochastic oscillator lines are above 80. A move out of the overbought zone would strengthen the signal for a resumption of the decline, with the 20 mark becoming the next reference point for the oscillator.

A close above 1.3125 on the hourly chart would postpone the intraday decline scenario and increase the likelihood of a deeper correction. In that case, the nearest recovery target would be the high of the previous upward move on the hourly chart, formed on 19 November.

Conclusion

GBP/USD has fallen to its lowest level in almost a year, weighed down by sharply rising expectations of further Fed tightening, with December rate hike probabilities now at 97.3% for a 25-basis-point move. While the Bank of England also expects inflation to accelerate, stable components in the October CPI and falling gilt yields have led markets to scale back BoE rate hike expectations, further weighing on the pound. The fundamental balance remains firmly in the dollar’s favour. Technically, the downtrend is intact, with resistance at 1.3125 and support at 1.3078 and 1.3024. A break below 1.3078 would open the way towards 1.3024 and potentially 1.2980, with the longer-range target at 1.2584. The Brutal (& Stealthy) Tech Bear Market

Having traded a plethora of difficult market environments, including COVID, the Global Financial Crisis, the Tariff Tantrum, and the 2022 bear market, I can confidently say that the 2026 market is one of the most difficult trading environments I can remember – if not the most difficult. The choppiness, whiplash, and violent direction changes make navigation challenging. Additionally, the sheer number of crosscurrents is more than I can ever remember. Until recently, higher oil prices and inflation concerns from the Iran War have weighed down stocks. Although oil prices have cooled significantly in recent weeks, the focus has turned to the AI trade. Despite unprecedented CAPEX spending, AI stocks have plunged.

Currently, the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index ETF (QQQ - Free Report) is ~15% off its all-time highs, triggering a market correction. While QQQ has yet to trigger a technical bear market (defined as a 20% drawdown from highs), most AI stocks have been pummeled and are already in bear-market territory. Below are some examples of AI stocks and their % off highs:

Nvidia (NVDA - Free Report): -40%

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD - Free Report): -26%

SanDisk (SNDK - Free Report) -68%

Nebius Group (NBIS - Free Report): -68%

Arm Holdings (ARM - Free Report): -61%

The Tech Trade is Reaching a Tipping Point

As the old Wall Street saying goes, “Sometimes when you try to pick bottoms, all you end up with is stinky fingers.” Currently, the bears are firmly in control of the market. The Nasdaq is below the 200-day moving average, AI’s most important CEO is out of a job, and interest rates are expected to keep moving higher. For intermediate-term investors, it’s critical to first and foremost protect capital and wait for confirmation in the form of improved market breadth and price rotation on higher time frames. If you need to reduce portfolio size, do so. The market is not going anywhere. Until then, avoid picking up pennies in front of a steamroller.

Nevertheless, if there’s one thing that I have learned throughout my years of investing experience, it’s that even if you’re a spectator, the market is still worth following closely. That’s because crisis ultimately equates to opportunity. Throughout American history, the market always exits these tough environments leading to massive opportunities. Additionally, equity markets are the master manipulator - bottoms are never obvious and often occur when they are least expected.

Market Extremes Pile Up

On Thursday, several extremes occurred on Wall Street, including:

·       Tech Valuations Reach Pandemic Lows: The S&P 500 Info Tech Index’s price-to-earnings ratio has plunged to 15x.

Image Source: Bloomberg

·       Rare, Violent Reversal: According to my friends at BlueKurtic Market Insights (@Bluekurtic), when QQQ starts the day 1.5% and finishes red, the chances of a low actually increase. Since 2010, QQQ was higher 5 days out in all 7 cases, with no further downside in 6. There were few such days around Dotcom and GFC, but they weren't so kind. (Counterintuitive, I know).

Image Source: Bluekurtic Market Insights

·       TICK Prints Multi-Month Lows: The TICK is a real-time market breadth indicator that measures short-term buying versus selling pressure on the New York Stock Exchange. On Thursday, TICK reached its most extreme selling level (-1448) in months. Often, a TICK washout of this nature is needed to flush out the last remaining bulls.

Some Market Hurdles are About to Pass

Market headwinds such as the Jensen Huang Nvidia exit, Anthropic IPO, and options expiration may provide much-needed relief for bulls. Huang was undoubtedly the most critical CEO for the tech trade. According to Elon Musk and others, he’s one of one. However, as investors come to terms with his exit, it’s worth noting that time is the ultimate healer.

Anthropic (ANT - Free Report), one of the most anticipated IPOs in history, debuted this week.Priced at $83, ANT shares soared to ~$110 intraday before encountering profit-taking and reversing course. The average Anthropic employee is now worth an astonishing $40 million. Billions of shares traded hands, marking one of the busiest IPOs in history. Despite the hysteria, investors sold shares of their current holdings to invest in Anthropic, putting downward pressure on the rest of the market.

Finally, options expiration was on Friday. Options expiration frequently triggers market turning points because dealers unwinding or rolling large option hedges—alongside expiring gamma pin levels and pinning magnets—forcing rapid rebalancing in underlying shares and index futures that can either release pent-up directional momentum or spark sharp mean reversion once the distortion clears.

Bottom Line

For now, the name of the game is capital preservation. That said, investors should stay positive and open-minded as markets can change on a dime.

data.title: Japanese Yen Edges Higher As CPI Data Reinforces December BoJ Rate Hike Expectations
data.description:
The USD/JPY pair loses traction to around 159.20 during the early European trading hours on Friday. The Japanese Yen (JPY) edges higher against the US Dollar (USD) as Japan’s National Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation data boost expectations for Bank of Japan (BoJ) policy tightening.

Data released by the Japan Statistics Bureau on Friday showed that National Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation climbed to 2.3% YoY in October from 2.1% in September. Meanwhile, the core CPI, which strips out prices of food, rose 2.2% YoY in October, compared to 2.1% in the previous reading, below the market consensus of 2.3%. This figure exceeded the central bank's 2% target for the second straight month.

The index that strips ‌away the effects of both volatile fresh food and fuel, which is closely watched by the BoJ as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressures, increased 2.2% YoY in October, versus 2.4% prior.

Japan’s October inflation report is likely to push the BoJ toward another rate hike in December, despite an unexpected contraction in economic growth in the third quarter. Data from LSEG indicates that there is a 72% likelihood of a 25 basis points (bps) hike from the Japanese central bank.

On Thursday, BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said that underlying inflation roughly aligns with the price target. He added that the central bank plans to continue raising interest rates as monetary conditions remain accommodative.

USD/JPY tests 160 as BoJ signals December hike but flags yen risks

Strategists at Brown Brothers Harriman note that USD/JPY is “up and testing key resistance at 160.00,” with “higher US yields” keeping the pair “biased upward.” However, they caution that “intervention risk makes chasing gains beyond 160.00 a less attractive risk-reward trade.”

On the policy front, BBH highlights that BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda “reinforced expectations for a 25bps rate hike to 1.50% on December 18 (85% priced in).” Ueda “played down weak Q3 consumption spending, arguing the decline was in line with expectations and spending should recover.” He also “reiterated that financial conditions remain loose and warned that yen weakness could add to inflation pressures,” underscoring the central bank’s growing sensitivity to currency-driven price risks.

Ueda flags inflation overshoot risk as BoJ leans toward further tightening

Ueda’s 8/10 FXS Speechtracker score sits modestly above the historic 7.5/10 baseline, signalling a slightly more hawkish tilt as the Bank of Japan highlights both steady growth and “fragility” alongside a clear willingness to keep raising rates while financial conditions remain loose. Emphasis on underlying inflation aligning with the 2% target, the explicit risk of an inflation overshoot, and simulations showing accelerated ETF sales would not severely damage BoJ finances all reinforce a narrative that policy normalization can proceed without destabilizing markets.

The repeated focus on a weak Yen amplifying inflation via broader price pass-through, and the admission that FX swings now matter more for long-term inflation expectations, underscore a growing sensitivity to currency-driven upside inflation risks that supports a hawkish bias. Still, acknowledgement that rising crude prices and a weak Yen could squeeze real incomes and damp consumption, plus data showing only steady consumption as wages rise, gives Ueda cover to keep rate hikes gradual and data-dependent, with the pace and timing explicitly tied to the probability of the baseline outlook and associated risks.

Technical Analysis: USD/JPY maintains a constructive outlook above the 100-day SMA

In the daily chart, USD/JPY keeps a mild bullish bias as it holds above the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) and the Bollinger middle band, suggesting underlying demand on shallow pullbacks. The Relative Strength Index (14) at 55 stays in positive but not overbought territory, hinting that upside momentum is constructive yet not stretched.

On the topside, immediate resistance is aligned with the upper Bollinger band near 160.30, where buyers could face profit-taking and volatility expansion. On the downside, initial support is seen at the 100-day SMA at 158.85, followed by the Bollinger mid-line at 158.65; a deeper retracement toward the lower Bollinger band around 157.00 would be needed to undermine the prevailing constructive tone.

data.title: Bitcoin Falls With Stocks Again: A Link That Only Began In 2020 Is Getting Tighter
data.description:
Bitcoin dropped to $61,291 on November 20, extending a slide that started when US stocks peaked on October 6. Since that day, the largest crypto has lost 28%, while the Nasdaq Composite is down 13.5% and the S&P 500 8.2% through Thursday’s close.

On Thursday alone, the day Anthropic listed on Nasdaq, the S&P 500 fell 2% for its sixth straight loss, and BTC slipped under $62,000.

The two markets are falling in step, and that wasn’t always the case. We measured how closely BTC and the Nasdaq have moved day to day since 2015. For its first years, Bitcoin went its own way. Since 2020, it has traded more and more like a tech stock, and over the past 40 trading days the link has been stronger than in any full calendar year.

So which stocks are hurting most, and why does crypto now fall with them?

AI and Crypto Stocks Lead the Sell-Off

We checked how 45 large AI, chip and crypto-related stocks have done since the October 6 peak. The worst performers fall into a few groups, and most of them sit right where AI and crypto overlap:

  • Miners turned AI landlords: bitcoin miners that now rent their power and buildings to AI companies fell the most. Bitdeer is down 69%, IREN 65%, Cipher Mining 58% and CleanSpark 53%.

  • AI cloud firms: Nebius lost 61% and CoreWeave 51%. Both rent out Nvidia chips to AI customers.

  • Crypto treasury companies: firms that hold crypto on their books dropped about twice as much as BTC itself. Strategy fell 48%, SharpLink 48% and BitMine 43%.

  • Crypto platforms: Galaxy lost 44%, Coinbase 41%, Robinhood 39% and stablecoin issuer Circle 38%.

  • Chips: Arm is down 41%, Nvidia 39% and Micron 34%.

The biggest names held up far better. Microsoft is down 6%, Tesla 2%, Amazon is flat and Apple is up 5%.

Nvidia is at the center of the AI slide. CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week amid a personal scandal, and the chipmaker has lost $735 billion in market value since it broke, the Associated Press reported. Worries that AI stocks had run too high added to the pressure. So did new US limits on remote access to advanced chips and talk of curbs on new data centers after this month’s midterm elections. “The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said.

Rates aren’t helping either. The 10-year Treasury yield sits above 5%, and inflation is running at 3.1%.

Bitcoin and the Nasdaq Barely Moved Together Before 2020

To answer whether crypto and stocks always moved together, we compared BTC’s daily price changes with those of the Nasdaq Composite, year by year since 2015. The measure, called correlation, runs from 1 (always moving together) to 0 (no link) and -1 (always moving in opposite directions).

  • 2015 to 2019: the correlation stayed between -0.11 and 0.08. The coin rose and crashed on its own news, with almost no tie to stocks.

  • 2020 onward: it jumped to 0.45 in the Covid year and has stayed positive since, peaking at 0.60 in 2022, when rising interest rates sank both markets.

  • Not a straight line: the link loosened to 0.19 in 2023, then climbed back to 0.47 in 2025.

  • Right now: over the last 40 trading days, it reached 0.65, above any full calendar year. The record for a 40-day stretch is still 0.81, set in May 2022.

So the answer is no. Crypto and stocks didn’t always move together. It’s a habit that started in 2020 and has grown stronger this year.

Big Investors Now Hold BTC Next to Tech Stocks

Several changes since 2020 explain why Bitcoin now trades like a risky tech stock:

  • The same buyers: hedge funds, wealth managers and pension funds now hold BTC, often through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) launched in January 2024. When they cut risk, they tend to sell both crypto and tech at once.

  • The same fuel: cheap money pushed both markets higher in 2020 and 2021. Higher rates pulled both down in 2022, and the prospect of more rate hikes is weighing on both now.

  • The same companies: many listed firms now straddle both worlds. Miners host AI data centers, and treasury companies like Strategy trade as stocks while holding crypto.

That last group shows the link most clearly. When AI shares fell, the miners that rent space to AI firms fell harder than either the coin or Nvidia.

Bitcoin Price Analysis: $62,300 Is The First Test For Bulls

On the daily chart, BTC trades at $61,859. That is below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $74,655, and its 200-day EMA at $75,470.

  • Resistance: $62,300, the floor BTC held in June, July, August and twice this month, now acting as a ceiling. Above that, $65,500.

  • Support: $58,500, where BTC turned in June and again on July 1.

BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: TradingView

As long as Bitcoin keeps moving with the Nasdaq, the next clue for BTC may come from tech stocks, starting with Nvidia. A calmer week for AI shares would give $58,500 a better chance to hold. Another leg down in tech would likely drag crypto with it.
